title: Tipped for drop but sitting top - St Mirren defying expectations
description: St Mirren were many people's favourites for relegation, so how come they have started with two opening wins in the Scottish Premiership?
fullText:
The start of a new season offers the chance to reset and St Mirren are taking full advantage. They are top of the table after two opening Scottish Premiership wins having defeated Falkirk and now St Johnstone without conceding.

It is in stark contrast to last term, when the Paisley side flirted with relegation, coming through a play-off to retain their top-flight status.

Off the back of that, there seemed little confidence among supporters and observers ahead of this campaign that a new dawn and return to the punching-above-their-weight campaigns of Stephen Robinson's tenure would be forthcoming.

It is very early days, of course, but the signs are St Mirren have regained many of the elements that have made them a real force in recent times.

Getting back to basics seems key for last seasons' League Cup winners, according to manager Craig McLeish. That and using the negative feeling that play-off last season brought as motivation.

"I'm still using that as fuel," he told BBC Scotland. "I don't want to be involved in that.

"We've got a massive journey ahead of us and we have to keep building. Six points out of six is a great start.

"It helps with the belief in each other. I've said to the boys I have confidence in them.

"Last season, we had two horrendous play-off games - even the emotion about it, there were so much nerves when we stepped on the pitch.

"We have to be horrible to play against. Two clean sheets sets us up well for that.

"We want to be really good at the basics and not get bored of that.

"The running, energy and desire. We want to be fit and strong and relentless this season against whoever we play. We have to keep those standards really high. We did it last week and lived up to it again."

It is a sentiment shared by new goalkeeping recruit Jacob Chapman, whose penalty save early in the second half laid the platform before Killian Phillips converted from the spot.

"Defenders throwing their bodies on the line; [Alex] Gogic throwing his head here and everywhere," he told BBC Scotland.

"Even the attackers coming back and helping defend.

"It sets the tempo for the season. It doesn't mean you're going to win every game or even have a great season, but it definitely helps.

"And it's what a great season looks like at the start. We've started well.

"A bit scrappy in some areas and we need to clean that out, but there was still some really nice football getting played in certain areas."

St Mirren beat St Johnstone to maintain winning start

McLeish has not hidden from the idea that St Mirren's model is to develop and move players on.

The standout example right now is Killian Phillips, the 24-year-old midfielder who has scored all three of their Premiership goals this season and is a big influence on the team as a whole.

"He's at the stage right now where he's round about the 100-game mark for the club," he said.

"He'll be looking for the next step in his career.

"If he attracts interest, then great. We're doing our job. I'm doing my job.

"I believe that the longer he stays and plays with me and with us, I'll get him the best move he possibly can.

"And if that's this window then fine. If it's in January, if we get him to the end of the season, it's part of it and we have to be prepared for any outcome.

"But we're just delighted to have him as part of our group. He's a massive part of it. And, if he keeps playing like that, his future takes care of itself."

title: Jaissle starts with win but not planning to 'smash locker room'
description: It was a night which ended with Newcastle United lifting a trophy, but there was certainly no danger of head coach Matthias Jaissle getting carried away.
fullText:
It was a night which ended with Newcastle United lifting silverware, but there was certainly no danger of new head coach Matthias Jaissle getting carried away.

Not after defeating Valencia in his first pre-season friendly in charge at the Mestalla Stadium.

"We will not smash the locker room now and celebrate a lot," he said after the 2-1 Orange Trophy win. "We still have a lot to work on."

That was quickly apparent after Newcastle fell behind inside four minutes, following Filip Ugrinic's curling opener.

But Jaissle will have taken heart from his players' response in a feisty contest, not least after Anthony Elanga was stretchered off following a bad tackle from Jose Gaya, which earned the Spaniard a red card.

Although Jaissle readily admitted he was "in fear" after seeing Elanga in distress, the Newcastle forward was walking a little later and it is not thought to be a serious injury after he bruised his shin.

Newcastle could have lost their heads, but striker Yoane Wissa came off the bench to score two goals, while fellow substitutes Bazoumana Toure and Sean Steur also caught the eye following their summer moves from Hoffenheim and Ajax respectively.

"Winning games always helps to gain confidence," Jaissle said. "We also knew that we had a hard week behind us.

"The players did well and there was a huge commitment to see in each session, so they really deserve two days off and then we start again."

Wissa & Toure star as Jaissle wins first Newcastle friendly - ratings

Inside Newcastle 2.0 - how the project is changing

There has been little time to waste following a period of dramatic change at the club.

Former head coach Eddie Howe has moved on and key players Alexander Isak, Bruno Guimaraes, Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon have all left in the last year.

Gallows humour gripped some supporters who made the trip after they adapted a chant which once featured the names of Guimaraes and Isak, who are now with Arsenal and Liverpool.

"We've got someone in the middle," they sang. "He knows exactly what we need. [Sven] Botman at the back, someone in attack, Newcastle are going to win the Premier League."

But it is not hard to imagine those blanks being filled in as a new generation steps up.

The average age of the squad has been dramatically lowered and 28-year-old forward Harvey Barnes was Newcastle's oldest starter against Valencia.

It felt like a potential sign of things to come on a night goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek, 24, midfielder Aladji Bamba, 20 and forward Toure, 20, made their debuts and 18-year-old Steur impressed from the bench.

Jaissle has a history of developing young players at RB Salzburg, which was a big draw for Newcastle, and he knows better than most what they need.

"Time is the key," Jaissle said. "They're young lads. It's never going to be easy in football, especially at the highest level, but we're here to do that."

Malick Thiaw was among the elder statesmen as he led Newcastle out as captain on his 25th birthday and this side will certainly need youthful vigour to play Jaissle's intense brand of football.

Jaissle was a vocal presence throughout on Saturday, urging the visitors up the field, and rarely stood within the markings of his technical area.

He was even running down the touchline in tandem with his players as they advanced on goal at times.

Just as there is a fine balance to strike on the field with such an aggressive approach, the same can be said off it.

Newcastle are in the market for additional experience, particularly in the middle of the park, and veterans Dan Burn and Fabian Schar will remain important voices in the dressing room.

But Jaissle has also shown the first sign of a ruthless streak.

Nick Pope was a pivotal figure under his predecessor, but the German left the 34-year-old out of the squad altogether against Valencia.

"I had a talk with Nick," Jaissle said. "I really appreciate what he did in his career so far.

"He knows exactly the situation right now and we need to deal with it in the best possible way, but I always appreciate the player and the human being behind."

Further changes are clearly coming and Jaissle now travels to Newcastle for the first time as head coach.

The 38-year-old already has a landmark in mind to see before he is formally unveiled at St James' Park next week.

"For sure I will be visiting the stadium and getting my first impressions," he said.

title: Tielemans cameo against PSG hints at Man Utd future
description: Manchester United's £35m signing Youri Tielemans makes an impressive debut in the 1-1 friendly draw against Paris St-Germain in Gothenburg.
fullText:
The sample size was only 26 minutes.

Yet the little combinations between Youri Tielemans and Bruno Fernandes after both were introduced in the second half of Manchester United's 1-1 draw with Paris St-Germain in Gothenburg drew an appreciative response from senior figures at the club.

With much made of United's activity - or lack of - in the transfer market this summer, it was good timing that Tielemans could make his debut when Mason Mount, arguably the club's player of pre-season, needed to be replaced after just 20 minutes.

Head coach Michael Carrick told Norwegian broadcaster VG post-match that Mount had come off as a precaution after taking a hefty blow to his foot. The former Chelsea midfielder walked freely past reporters to the team bus an hour after the final whistle.

Nevertheless, Tielemans was a surprise signing when Manchester United triggered a previously unknown £35m clause in the Belgian's contract at Aston Villa to agree a five-year deal.

There was a lot of debate in the immediate aftermath about how much football the 29-year-old, who made his professional debut for Anderlecht when he was just 16, had played.

Against PSG he did not do anything particularly special.

There were a couple of 45-yard cross-field passes that found their intended targets. There were some simple first-time lay-offs to team-mates within 10 yards.

There was also a short sprint just outside the United area to close down dangerman Khvicha Kvaratskhelia when Tielemans recognised the PSG star could be about to take possession within shooting distance.

He got there, won the ball and played a simple pass, taking the ball out of harm's way.

'Tidy debut' for Tielemans - how Man Utd rated against PSG

This isn't really what got the United contingent purring.

They were reacting to the little passes between Tielemans and Fernandes, which allowed United to ease their way out of trouble or move up the pitch.

Fernandes was the key man last season as United finished third. Nine goals and 21 assists was a decisive contribution in returning the club to the Champions League after a two-year absence.

Tielemans showed in his brief cameo he can take some of the pressure off the Portuguese.

"Youri has consistently been one of the most outstanding midfielders in the Premier League throughout the past seven years," said director of football Jason Wilcox on Tielemans' signing.

"He will add further composure, creativity and leadership to our squad.

"He has all of the technical qualities, as well as the ambition and mentality, to thrive at Manchester United."

If Wilcox reflects on those words as United head off to the Republic of Ireland for their week-long training camp in Maynooth, he can be quite pleased with himself.

It was only 26 minutes, but on that evidence, he has got it spot on.

Carrick has confirmed Marcus Rashford will rejoin the Manchester United squad for their trip to the Republic of Ireland.

Rashford, England team-mate Kobbie Mainoo and Argentina defender Lisandro Martinez are the final three players to return for United after the World Cup.

Although it was not expected Rashford would return to the club when he joined Barcelona on loan in July 2025, the La Liga champions failed to trigger a £26m option to buy the 28-year-old at the end of the season.

Despite interest elsewhere, there has been no deal, meaning Rashford will return to United for the first time since January 2025, when he moved to Aston Villa after falling out with former manager Ruben Amorim.

United are training at the plush Carton House hotel in Maynooth and have a friendly with Leeds United at Croke Park on 12 August.

They complete their pre-season programme against Amorim's new club AC Milan in Wroclaw on 15 August, when Rashford could make his first United appearance since December 2024 if Carrick decides Wednesday is too soon.

A former team-mate, coach and manager of Rashford, it has been felt if anyone can patch up the relationship between club and player - which includes his number 10 shirt being given to Matheus Cunha who is also due to be on the trip after a minor injury ruled him out of the Gothenburg encounter - it is Carrick.

"I've played with him. I played in the game he made his debut, so we have a history," Carrick said.

"We have got a full squad this week in Dublin. We fly straight there and have a few days where we have the whole group back together. Marcus is part of that, and Kobbie [Mainoo] and Lisandro [Martinez]. We look forward to seeing them."

title: Simpson avenges only loss in Williamson rematch
description: Callum Simpson reclaims the British and Commonwealth super-middleweight titles as he earns a unanimous decision in his rematch with Troy Williamson.
fullText:
Callum Simpson reclaimed the British and Commonwealth super-middleweight titles after earning a unanimous decision in his rematch with Troy Williamson.

The impressive Simpson avenged the only loss of his career, when Williamson upset the odds to stop him in the 10th round in December.

The English pair put on another thrilling contest in Leeds which the judges scored 116-112, 117-112 and 115-113 in Simpson's favour.

The 29-year-old, fighting under new trainer Rob McCracken, rocked Williamson with a big right hand in the third round.

But Williamson, 34, hung in and stung the challenger in the eighth round. Then, knowing he needed a knockout, he took the fight to Simpson in the final round.

However, that late rally was not enough to stop Yorkshire's Simpson improving his professional record to 19 wins and one loss.

"It feels amazing," said Simpson. "I really didn't want it to be that exciting, but Troy is a tough fighter. He won the last fight so he [had] every right to be confident.

"What everyone doesn't know is that, in the last fight, I perforated both my eardrums in the first round. I was an absolute mess so that fight for me was just trying to survive.

"But I didn't make any excuses. I've come back better, learned from it and I knew I was going to get the win tonight."

Simpson's promoter Ben Shalom said the fight was "unbelievable" and praised Williamson, now 22-5 with one draw, as he "kept coming".

But Shalom feels Simpson is back in world-title contention and hopes to secure him a shot in the next 12 months.

"In boxing, people are so quick to write someone off," he added. "The amount of people that told me 'do not take that rematch'.

"We took it, [Simpson] did it and I'm so happy for him."

title: Fifa criticises campaign to oust president Infantino
description: Fifa strongly criticises what it calls a "concerted and ongoing effort" to "undermine" the organisation and its president Gianni Infantino.
fullText:
Fifa has strongly criticised what it calls a "concerted and ongoing effort" to "undermine" the organisation and its president Gianni Infantino.

The statement follows a Daily Telegraph report, external which claimed Infantino's alleged lover was given a severance payment by Uefa after he had an affair while he was its general secretary.

A Fifa spokesperson told the Telegraph Infantino "strongly denies" the allegations and that they are "categorically untrue".

Fifa has now itself hit out at "unsubstantiated assertions and demonstrably false claims", adding that "speculation and insinuation should not be presented as fact".

Infantino has come under increasing pressure from Uefa and European football associations over his aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal.

FFE would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights, with 21% sold off to a private investment company.

Uefa has said it has lost confidence in Infantino, while Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) president Lise Klaveness on Friday called on the Swiss-Italian to resign.

European football's governing body says its threat to boycott Fifa events remains on the table, adding that assurances the FFE plan could not be revived have not been received.

"The Fifa president was democratically elected by Fifa's Member Associations and continues to serve with their mandate," Fifa said in its statement on Saturday.

"It is increasingly evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine Fifa and its president.

"Those who do not have the support of Fifa's member associations should not seek to achieve through allegation, insinuation or misinformation what they cannot achieve through Fifa's established democratic processes."

Opposition to Infantino is largely from within Europe.

The Mexican Football Federation broke ranks with its regional governing body Concacaf to come out in support of Infantino.

It echoed a statement from Conmebol - South America's governing body - in saying it would reject any attempt to remove Infantino without a vote involving all 211 Fifa member countries.

Infantino is also unanimously backed by the 54 nations of the Confederation of African Football (Caf).

Infantino called members of the Fifa management board to a meeting in Rabat, Morocco on Wednesday.

Fifa issued a statement on behalf of Infantino and secretary general Mattias Grafstrom which apologised for the FFE proposal, but also said it would "no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process".

The statement released late on Saturday evening was similarly defensive about the criticism the organisation has faced.

"Change inevitably challenges established interests, but disagreement with that change cannot justify efforts to undermine the democratic mandate of Fifa's president or the institution he was elected to lead," it added.

"Fifa welcomes legitimate scrutiny. But scrutiny is not a licence to distort facts, amplify unsubstantiated allegations or manufacture distractions designed to undermine progress.

"Where reporting is inaccurate or misleading, Fifa will challenge it directly and vigorously."

title: Hillary Clinton calls out far-left reluctance to support her, warns GOP 'communist' attacks will be effective
description: Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton warns progressives' refusal to back establishment Democrats after primaries creates a costly one-way street.
fullText:
The tensions between the far-left and more establishment wings of the Democratic Party are not going away, as evidenced by some sharp comments from former presidential nominee Hillary Clinton this week.

Clinton lamented during an interview Friday that the far left doesn't fall in line and support establishment Democrats as figures like Hasan Piker are demanding fealty, while also warning Republican attacks on hard-left socialists could be "very effective."

"Pivot" podcast host Kara Swisher noted to Clinton that the Democratic Party is having a tense internal struggle between its more establishment and progressive wings to the point that Republican opposition has learned to capitalize on it.

"I think there's no doubt that, you know, the Republican Party is the Trump cult and the Democratic Party is a bigger tent. You know, we do have a broad cross-section of people, what they believe, what their experiences are. I think that's an advantage," Clinton said. "But we also have to win general elections."

2026 Midterms State Of Play: Key Races Unfold As Stevens, El-sayed Battle In Michigan

Clinton noted that many Democrats now will have to learn to pivot and support the progressive Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed's campaign to defeat Republican Mike Rogers, while El-Sayed's supporters will have to learn how to reintegrate defeated Haley Stevens and her supporters who they were "vilifying" online and in person.

Clinton warned that the Democratic Party's coalition cannot afford to keep being a one-way street in supporting candidates.

"One thing that we haven't yet seen enough of is that when the progressives, the left — whatever we want to call, you know, candidates on that side of the Democratic Party — when they lose, they often don't support the candidate that has been nominated," she said. "You know, there was a lot of reluctance to support Kamala Harris. There was a lot of reluctance to support me when I got the nomination. So, it can't be a one-way street.

"If we're going to have a fair election, as there was in Michigan, and somebody comes out ahead, a little bit ahead, but needs to get a huge percentage of the voters that voted for Haley, they're going to have to be willing to, you know, get in — get into a conversation that brings those people over," she added, noting that the real struggle will be persuading independents and Stevens supporters.

Rogers Opens Door To Democratic Voters After El-sayed's Primary Victory: 'There Is Still Hope'

Clinton went on to remark on the Republican messaging of accusing people of being a "communist" or "socialist," adding, "I assume that they have reason to believe that it's effective, or they wouldn't be beating the drum on it."

"And you can see that it's not just about Michigan, but the Republican messaging is communist, socialist. It's going to be a very effective attack," she said.

Even so, she said, such "scare tactics" did not stop the rise of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

Clinton warned again that when moderates pivot to support progressive nominees, the progressive nominee needs to make sure that those moderates feel welcomed, adding, "Look, we've got to work together. We're not going to beat Republicans by being divided."

James Carville, who helped mastermind Bill Clinton's 1992 election victory, told Fox News Digital this week the 2028 primary would be a true test of the strength of the far left in the party. Carville has warned that he could leave the party if it makes room for extreme figures like Piker, who campaigned with El-Sayed.

title: With broad bipartisan support, Congress is about to give Trump ‘unchecked authority’ to impose new tariffs of up to 100% on top trading partners
description: "We should not have to choose between putting a check on Putin's aggression and putting a check on this president's tariffs regime."
fullText:
Courts have blocked President Donald Trump's earlier attempts to use existing laws for his trade war, but Congress is advancing a new law that would provide broad discretion to impose steep tariffs.

In an 86-to-11 vote, the Senate passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026 on Friday, with the House expected to approve the bill with similar bipartisan support next month.

It sanctions Russian President Vladimir Putin and senior Kremlin officials while also targeting the country's energy sector to cripple the economy amid its war on Ukraine.

The bill would let Trump impose fresh tariffs as high as 100% on the top five importers of Russian oil and gas. While that could include U.S. allies like the European Union, South Korea, Japan as well as top trading partners like China and India, the president also has the ability to issue waivers if he deems it "in the national interest of the United States."

Despite the overwhelming support, Sens. Rand Paul, R-Ky., and Ron Wyden, D-Ore., tried to remove the bill's tariff authority, but failed.

"It will not bring peace to Ukraine, but rather will deliberately make American families poorer by increasing tariffs, which are nothing but a tax on imported goods," Paul said on the Senate floor.

Sen. Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., also balked at the tariff power but eventually voted for the bill after receiving a written promise from U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer that tariffs would be lifted after countries are no longer deemed top buyers of Russian energy or facilitators of sanctions evasion.

Still, he expressed unease about handing over sweeping new tariffs powers to Trump and vowed to remain vigilant.

"We should not have to choose between putting a check on Putin's aggression and putting a check on this president's tariffs regime," Warnock said, adding that if Trump "oversteps his power, we will see him in court."

The vote comes after the Supreme Court ruled in February that Trump can't use the International Emergency Economic Powers Act to impose his "Liberation Day" tariffs, upholding a series of lower-court rulings.

But he pivoted to Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 to impose temporary 10% tariffs, then invoked Section 301 of the same law for new levies of 10%-12-5% on 60 trading partners.

Those duties are also expected to face lawsuits as they're based on accusations of forced labor, even in top developed economies.

Tariffs under the Russia sanctions bill, however, would likely avoid similar legal challenges as it provides more open-ended authority to a president who has already tried to interpret trade laws extremely aggressively.

"The Russia bill is riddled with the same ambiguity the president has exploited in these other laws," Cato Institute scholars Clark Packard and Scott Lincicome wrote in a Washington Post op-ed last week.

They pointed out that the bill doesn't specify what data will determine which countries are the five largest importers of Russian energy. And while the tariff authority expires in five years, the bill doesn't say how long the tariffs themselves will last.

Tariffs exemptions are also not automatic and are subject to the USTR's determination that allies have taken "significant steps" to reduce their imports, Packard and Lincicome added. In addition, the tariff rates are at the president's whim.

"Trump could direct the trade representative to set the tariff rate at 100% for one buyer of Russian energy and zero for another. That unchecked authority gives Trump leverage in disputes unrelated to Ukraine," they warned.

For example, Trump could threaten India with new tariffs as part of trade talks that may cover farm exports, digital taxes or drug prices.

The ability to hit China with a new 100% U.S. tariff could also upset the fragile trade truce the world's two biggest economies have been observing for the past year.

But even as Packard and Lincicome accuse Trump of abusing "nearly every tariff statute on the books," they place most of the blame on Congress.

The Russia sanctions bill merely marks the latest instance of the legislative branch ceding trade authority to the executive branch.

"For more than half a century, Congress has delegated broad tariff powers to the president with few limitations," they explained. "If the president has run wild, it's only because lawmakers took away the guardrails."

This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: He's been frozen on Everest for 30 years, now 'Green Boots' may finally be coming home
description: For decades, an Indian man's lime shoes have been a grim trail marker for many climbing the world's highest peak.
fullText:
For 30 years, a dead body known as "Green Boots" has been lying in the snow, nestled under an overhanging rock, not far from Mount Everest's summit.

The lime mountaineering boots worn by an Indian climber who died in 1996 have been a grim trail marker for many climbers on their way up the world's highest peak ever since.

Now India is looking for a specialist high-altitude recovery team to undertake a complex and risky mission to retrieve what they say is Dorje Morup's body – arguably the most famous of the hundreds whose bodies have been left frozen on the mountain.

Warning: This story contains a picture of a dead body.

They hope they are on the cusp of returning his remains to friends and family who never gave up hope he'd come home.

"On some days, before I went to sleep, I would think that there'd be a knock on the door tonight and that when I opened, he would be there," Morup's wife told the BBC.

"When he comes home, I will ask him: 'Where were you all these years?'"

The night before he left to be part of a historic Indian expedition on Everest, Morup sat with his wife at his home in Ladakh, an Indian-administered territory in another part of the Himalayas.

He made her a promise: that he would come back a hero and make his country proud.

"He asked me to take care of the kids and come to the airport to greet him on his return," Konchak Yangskit told the BBC at her home.

A lance naik, or lance corporal, in the Indo Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), the force guarding much of India's border with China, 48-year-old Morup was no stranger to Himalayan trekking.

But Yangskit says she had a strange sense of foreboding that night: "I wondered if I was ever going to see him again."

Morup was one of six climbers on the ITBP expedition attempting to reach the top of Everest – which lies on the border between Nepal and the Chinese-governed territory of Tibet.

Most climbers choose to ascend from the Nepalese side, but Morup's crew wanted to write their names into the history books as the first Indian expedition to do it from the treacherous Chinese side.

Three out of six members of the expedition turned back due to a snowstorm, but Morup and two others - Tsewang Smanla and Tsewang Paljor – kept struggling, all the way up to the 8,849m summit.

Disaster, a blizzard, struck as they descended and killed all three.

Like many of the more than 300 people who have died in the Everest region since records began a century ago, their bodies remain on the mountain.

Two have never been found, but the third body - that of "Green Boots" - has been lying frozen in the snow for three decades at an altitude of 8,500 metres.

For years, it was assumed that "Green Boots" was another member of the expedition, Tsewang Paljor.

But testimony from surviving members of the 1996 expedition and the location of the last radio contact with the climbers have now led authorities to believe the remains belong to Morup.

An ITBP official, speaking anonymously because he is not authorised to speak to the media, told BBC News Hindi that Morup's clothes and climbing gear helped officials identify the body in recent years.

Since then, they've been plotting how to get their comrade home so they can confirm his identity beyond doubt through DNA testing and offer his family a semblance of closure.

"We never forgot him. It was only a matter of time," the ITBP official said.

Retrieving those who have died on the mountain is a dangerous, gruelling task, and, up until the past decade, very rare.

Many of the bodies, like Morup's, are in what climbers call Everest's death zone – where temperatures can plunge to -40C and oxygen levels are about a third of those at sea level.

"The weather and snow conditions are going to be crucial," said Tshiring Jangbu Sherpa, a prominent Nepalese mountaineer who has taken part in other recovery missions.

"The north side has fewer crevasses, but it is riskier. If something bad happens from the Nepalese side, you get quickly evacuated by helicopter. But there is no such system from the Chinese side," he told BBC Hindi.

The Chinese side of the peak – where Green Boots' body is – is steeper and doesn't have the same support structures as the southern slope, which is another complicating factor, Sherpa sources have told BBC News Nepali.

"It's really tough to get that body down even in popular spring season, let alone the autumn [which has more unpredictable weather]. That's the simple reason it is still there for so many years," mountaineering guide Pemba Ongchu Sherpa said.

"There would need to be 10 to 12 climbers who are capable of making summits, just to fix [support] ropes to reach that point."

Green Boots will also have to be physically carried down to an altitude where it can be collected by a helicopter, or possibly yaks, and transported back to an airport – a job which also requires huge manpower.

Sherpas say bodies shrouded in iced-up climbing gear often weigh several times the average man and are frequently frozen into awkward positions, making bringing them down the challenging terrain even more treacherous. The remains may also begin defrosting and decomposing once they reach lower altitudes.

The start of the descent with the body would be the most difficult, Indian climber Kuntal Joisher told BBC Nepali.

"It's going to be very, very risky endeavour. It's extremely steep ground with lots of rock. Logistically, this [first] 1000m is going to be a humungous challenge."

"The main thing is to not put Sherpa lives at risk for a dead body."

All of this makes for a hugely expensive recovery mission – experts say even the most straightforward ones cost between $40,000 and $80,000, a sum beyond the means of most families.

It is more common for local teams to move people who have died out of view on the mountain: like explorer Francys Arsentiev, dubbed the Sleeping Beauty of Everest, who in 2007 was moved to a more private final resting place on Everest almost a decade after she died.

But the ITBP – which is funding the recovery operation – wants Morup's body to be returned by September, and is looking for mountain rescue Sherpa groups who could do the job.

Once returned to India, the body will undergo DNA testing and, if confirmed to be Morup, his remains will be given back to his family.

For years, Morup's family back in Ladakh have struggled to come to terms with his disappearance.

Now around 75, Yangskit struggles to recall even the day she was married. But the days after the tragedy remain etched in her mind.

"I only knew there was a storm on the mountain. Even though we organised cremation prayers at home, my heart refused to believe he had died," she says with tears rolling down her face.

"I didn't see his dead body, so it was difficult for me to believe it."

All that remains of Morup today are his medals and trophies, a couple of old photos from his mountain adventures – and, most importantly, a certificate from the Chinese government which states that at 17:30 on 10 May 1996, Morup reached the top of Everest.

If the recovery mission is successful, Morup's son Punchok Dorjai told the BBC that the family would hold a funeral for him near the Martyrs Park in Ladakh's capital Leh.

"My father gave his life for the country and he should be remembered as a martyr," Dorjai said, adding that his teammates who perished deserve the same title.

The family will also proudly save a symbol of Morup's legacy at their home, to go alongside his summit certification, he said: "We are planning to keep the Green Boots."

Additional reporting by Pradeep Bashyal, BBC News Nepali
